# The Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order 2005

At the Court at Buckingham Palace, the 9th day of February 2005

Present,

The Queen’s Most Excellent Majesty in Council

Whereas in pursuance of section 3(1) of the Parliamentary Constituencies Act 1986([1](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/250/made#f00001 "Go to footnote 1")) the Boundary Commission for Scotland have submitted to the Secretary of State a report dated 30th November 2004 showing the constituencies into which they recommend, in accordance with that Act, that Scotland should be divided:

And whereas the Secretary of State has laid that report before Parliament together with the draft of this Order in Council to give effect, without modifications, to the recommendations contained in the report and each House of Parliament has by resolution approved the said draft:

Now, therefore, Her Majesty, in pursuance of section 4 of the Parliamentary Constituencies Act 1986 and of all other powers enabling Her in that behalf, is pleased, by and with the advice of Her Privy Council, to order, and it is hereby ordered, as follows:–

1.—(1) This Order may be cited as the Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order 2005.

(2) Subject to section 4(6) of the Parliamentary Constituencies Act 1986, this Order shall come into force on the day after the day on which it is made.

(3) In this Order–

(a)any reference to a ward is a reference to the ward of the local government area in which that ward is situated; and

(b)any reference to a local government area is a reference to that area as it existed on 30th November 2004.

2. Scotland shall be divided into the constituencies–

(a)which are named in column 1 of the Schedule to this Order;

(b)which comprise the areas which are set out in column 2 of that Schedule opposite the name of the constituency; and

(c)which are designated as being either county constituencies or burgh constituencies according to the name in column 1 of that Schedule.

3. Each electoral registration officer for the constituencies referred to in Article 2 above shall make such re-arrangement or adaptation of the registers of parliamentary electors as may be necessary to give effect to this Order.

4. The Parliamentary Constituencies (Scotland) Order 1995([2](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/250/made#f00002 "Go to footnote 2")) is revoked.

A. K. Galloway

Clerk of the Privy Council

A [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_elections_in_the_United_Kingdom "General elections in the United Kingdom") was held in the United Kingdom on 12 December 2019, with 47,074,800 registered voters[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-7) entitled to vote to elect 650 [Members of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MPs) to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"). The governing [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)"), led by [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom")[Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson"), won a [landslide victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") with a majority of 80 seats,[[n 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-8) a net gain of 48, on 43.6 per cent of the popular vote, the highest percentage for any party since the [1979 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_United_Kingdom_general_election "1979 United Kingdom general election").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Boris_Elec_2019-9) This was the second national election to be held in 2019 in the United Kingdom, the first being the [2019 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom").

After it lost its parliamentary majority at the [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), the Conservative Party governed in minority with the support of the [Democratic Unionist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party "Democratic Unionist Party") (DUP). The prime minister, [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May"), resigned in July 2019 after repeatedly failing to pass her [Brexit withdrawal agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Brexit withdrawal agreement") in parliament. Johnson succeeded her as the [leader of the Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Conservative Party (UK)") and as prime minister in July 2019. Johnson could not persuade Parliament to approve a revised withdrawal agreement by the end of October, and chose to call a [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election"), which the House of Commons supported under the [Early Parliamentary General Election Act 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Parliamentary_General_Election_Act_2019 "Early Parliamentary General Election Act 2019").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-:3-10) Opinion polls showed a firm lead for the Conservatives against the opposition Labour Party throughout the campaign.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-11)

The Conservatives won 365 seats, their highest number and proportion since the [1987 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_United_Kingdom_general_election "1987 United Kingdom general election"), and recorded their highest share of the popular vote since 1979; many of their gains were made in seats once considered safe for Labour, dubbed the [red wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_wall_(British_politics) "Red wall (British politics)"), which had voted strongly in favour of British withdrawal from the EU in the [2016 European Union (EU) membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum"). Labour won 202 seats, its fewest since the [1935 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_United_Kingdom_general_election "1935 United Kingdom general election").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-12)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-13)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Corbyn_Defeat-14) The [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) made a net gain of 13 seats with 45 per cent of the vote in Scotland, winning 48 of the 59 seats there.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Sturgeon_2019_Elec-15) The [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") increased their vote share to 11.6 per cent, but won only 11 seats, a net loss of one since the last election. The party's leader, [Jo Swinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Swinson "Jo Swinson"), lost her seat to the SNP, thus triggering the [2020 party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Liberal_Democrats_leadership_election "2020 Liberal Democrats leadership election"), which was won by [Ed Davey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Davey "Ed Davey").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Swinson_Defeat-16)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-17) The DUP won a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting) "Plurality (voting)") of seats in Northern Ireland. The [Social Democratic and Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_and_Labour_Party "Social Democratic and Labour Party") (SDLP) and the [Alliance Party of Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Party_of_Northern_Ireland "Alliance Party of Northern Ireland") (APNI) regained parliamentary representation as the DUP lost seats.

The election result gave Johnson the mandate he sought from the electorate to formally implement the [withdrawal of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") from the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), and to complete the repeal of the [European Communities Act 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Communities_Act_1972_(UK) "European Communities Act 1972 (UK)") on 31 January 2020. [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"), Labour's leader at the election, resigned, triggering the [2020 party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2020 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), which was won by his shadow Brexit secretary, [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Corbyn_Defeat-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-18)[Jane Dodds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Dodds "Jane Dodds"), the Liberal Democrats' leader in Wales, was also unseated in [Brecon and Radnorshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecon_and_Radnorshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Brecon and Radnorshire (UK Parliament constituency)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-19) In Northern Ireland, [Irish nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_nationalist "Irish nationalist") MPs outnumbered [unionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unionism_in_Ireland "Unionism in Ireland") for the first time, although the unionist popular vote remained higher at 43.1 per cent, and the seven [Sinn Féin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinn_F%C3%A9in "Sinn Féin") MPs did not take their seats due to their tradition of [abstentionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstentionism "Abstentionism").

Despite being elected with a large majority, Johnson went on to resign amid a [government crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis "July 2022 United Kingdom government crisis") in 2022, being followed by [Liz Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss "Liz Truss") for [fifty days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis "October 2022 United Kingdom government crisis") and then by [Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak"), who went on to lead the Conservatives to a landslide defeat in the [subsequent election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"). This was the last election to be held under the reign of [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II").

In July 2016, [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") was elected [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") to succeed [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron"), who had resigned following the 2016 [Brexit referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_referendum "Brexit referendum"). The [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") had governed since the [2010 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election"), initially in coalition with the [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") and then alone with a small majority following the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). In the [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), May lost her majority but was able to resume office as a result of a [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") agreement with Northern Ireland's [Democratic Unionist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party "Democratic Unionist Party") (DUP), known as the [Conservative–DUP agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative%E2%80%93DUP_agreement "Conservative–DUP agreement"). In the face of opposition from the DUP and Conservative [backbenchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbencher "Backbencher"), the [second May ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_May_ministry "Second May ministry") was unable to pass its [Brexit withdrawal agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Brexit withdrawal agreement") by 29 March 2019, so some political commentators considered that an early general election was likely.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-20)

The opposition [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") called for a [2019 vote of confidence in the May ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_vote_of_confidence_in_the_May_ministry "2019 vote of confidence in the May ministry") but the motion, held in January, failed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-21) May resigned following her party's poor performance in the [2019 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom") during the first extension granted by the European Union for negotiations on the withdrawal agreement. [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") won the [2019 Conservative leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "2019 Conservative Party leadership election") and became the prime minister on 24 July 2019. Along with attempting to revise the withdrawal agreement arranged by his predecessor's negotiations, Johnson made three attempts to hold a snap election under the process defined in the [Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-term_Parliaments_Act_2011 "Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-22) which required a two-thirds [supermajority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermajority "Supermajority") in order for an election to take place.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-23)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-24)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-25)

All three attempts to call an election failed to gain support; Parliament insisted that Johnson "take a [no-deal Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-deal_Brexit "No-deal Brexit") off the table first" and secure a negotiated Withdrawal Agreement, expressed in particular by its enactment against his will of the [European Union (Withdrawal) (No. 2) Act 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_(Withdrawal)_(No._2)_Act_2019 "European Union (Withdrawal) (No. 2) Act 2019"), often called the Benn Act, after Labour MP [Hilary Benn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Benn "Hilary Benn"), who introduced the bill. After failing to pass a revised deal before the first extension's deadline of 31 October 2019, Johnson agreed to a second extension on negotiations with the European Union and finally secured a revised withdrawal agreement.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Parliament_breaks_deadlock-26)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Parliament_breaks_deadlock_2-27)

Parliament agreed to an election through a motion proposed by the Liberal Democrats and the [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") (SNP) on 28 October. The [Early Parliamentary General Election Act 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Parliamentary_General_Election_Act_2019 "Early Parliamentary General Election Act 2019") (EPGEA) was passed in the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") by 438 votes to 20; an attempt to pass an amendment by opposition parties for the election to be held on 9 December failed by 315 votes to 295.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Parliament_breaks_deadlock-26)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-Parliament_breaks_deadlock_2-27) The [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords") followed suit on 30 October,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-28) with [royal assent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_assent "Royal assent") made the day after for the ratification of the EPGEA.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-29)

The Conservative Party and Labour Party have been the two biggest political parties, and have supplied every Prime Minister since the [1922 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_United_Kingdom_general_election "1922 United Kingdom general election"). The Conservative Party had governed since the 2010 election, in coalition with the Liberal Democrats from 2010 to 2015. At the 2015 general election, the Conservative Party committed to offering a referendum on whether the United Kingdom should leave the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) and won a majority in that election. A referendum was held in June 2016, and the Leave campaign won by 51.9% to 48.1%.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-bbc240519-53)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-bbc230719-54)

[United Kingdom invocation of Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_invocation_of_Article_50_of_the_Treaty_on_European_Union "United Kingdom invocation of Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union") came in March 2017, and [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") triggered a [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election") in 2017, in order to demonstrate support for her planned negotiation of Brexit. Instead, the Conservative Party lost seats. They won a plurality of MPs but not a majority, and the result was a [hung parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hung_parliament "Hung parliament"). They formed a [minority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_government "Minority government"), with the [Democratic Unionist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party "Democratic Unionist Party") (DUP) as their [confidence and supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_and_supply "Confidence and supply") partner. Neither May nor her successor [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson"), the winner of the [2019 Conservative leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "2019 Conservative Party leadership election"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-bbc240519-53)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-bbc230719-54) was able to secure parliamentary support either for a deal on the terms of the country's exit from the EU, or for exiting the EU without an agreed deal. Johnson later succeeded in bringing his withdrawal agreement to a second reading in Parliament, following another extension until January 2020.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-55)

After Johnson's 2019 win, a new Withdrawal Agreement Bill was introduced in 2020. Compared to its 2019 October predecessor, this bill offered, in the words of political scientist [Meg Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meg_Russell "Meg Russell"), "significantly weaker parliamentary oversight of Brexit ... giving parliament no formal role in agreeing the future relationship negotiating objectives, and a diminished role in approving any resulting treaty."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-56)

During the lifespan of the 2017 Parliament, twenty MPs resigned from their parties, mostly due to disputes with their party leaderships; some formed new parties and alliances. In February 2019, eight Labour and three Conservative MPs left their parties to sit together as [The Independent Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent_Group "The Independent Group").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-57) Having undergone a split and two name changes, at dissolution, this group numbered five MPs who sat as the registered party The Independent Group for Change under the leadership of [Anna Soubry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Soubry "Anna Soubry").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-telegraph290319-58)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-59)

Two MPs sat in a group called [The Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independents_(UK) "The Independents (UK)"), which at its peak had five members. One MP created the [Birkenhead Social Justice Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkenhead_Social_Justice_Party "Birkenhead Social Justice Party"), while a further 20 MPs who began as Labour or Conservative ended Parliament as unaffiliated independents. Seven MPs, from both the Conservatives and Labour, joined the Liberal Democrats during Parliament, in combination with a gain after the [2019 Brecon and Radnorshire by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Brecon_and_Radnorshire_by-election "2019 Brecon and Radnorshire by-election"). By the time Parliament was dissolved, the Liberal Democrats had raised their number from 12 at the election to 20 at dissolution.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-60)

One reason for the defections from the Labour Party was the ongoing row over alleged [antisemitism in the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_Labour_Party "Antisemitism in the Labour Party"). Labour entered the election campaign while under investigation by the [Equality and Human Rights Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_and_Human_Rights_Commission "Equality and Human Rights Commission").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-61) The [Jewish Labour Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Labour_Movement "Jewish Labour Movement") declared that it would not generally campaign for Labour.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-62) The Conservative Party was also criticised for not doing enough to tackle the alleged [Islamophobia in the Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia_in_the_Conservative_Party "Islamophobia in the Conservative Party").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-63) The Conservatives ended the previous parliamentary period with fewer seats than they had started with because of defections and also saw the [2019 suspension of rebel Conservative MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_suspension_of_rebel_Conservative_MPs "2019 suspension of rebel Conservative MPs") for going against the party line by voting to prevent a [no-deal Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-deal_Brexit "No-deal Brexit").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-64) Of the 21 expelled, 10 were subsequently reinstated, while the others continued as independents.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-65)

### Policy positions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Policy positions")]

#### Brexit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Brexit")]

The major parties had a wide variety of stances on Brexit. The Conservative Party supported leaving under the terms of the withdrawal agreement as negotiated by Johnson (amending May's previous agreement), and this agreement formed a central part of the Conservative campaign via the slogan "[Get Brexit Done](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Brexit_Done "Get Brexit Done")".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-66) The [Brexit Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_Party "Brexit Party") was in favour of a no-deal Brexit, with its leader [Nigel Farage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Farage "Nigel Farage") calling for Johnson to drop the deal.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-67)

The Conservative manifesto read "If we elect a majority of Conservative MPs to Parliament, we will start putting our deal through Parliament before Christmas and we will leave the European Union in January" which ultimately happened.

The Labour Party proposed a renegotiation of the withdrawal agreement, towards a closer post-withdrawal relationship with the EU, and would then put this forward as an option in a referendum alongside the option of remaining in the EU.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-68) The Labour Party's campaigning stance in that referendum would be decided at a special conference.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-69) In a _Question Time_ special featuring four party leaders, Labour leader [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") said that he would stay neutral in the referendum campaign.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-70)

The [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)"), [Scottish National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party"), [Plaid Cymru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaid_Cymru "Plaid Cymru"), [The Independent Group for Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent_Group_for_Change "The Independent Group for Change"), and the [Green Party of England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales") were all opposed to Brexit, and proposed that a further referendum be held with the option, for which they would campaign, to remain in the EU.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-71) The Liberal Democrats originally pledged that if they formed a [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government"), which was considered a highly unlikely outcome by observers,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-72) they would revoke the Article 50 notification immediately and cancel Brexit.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-73)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-74) Part-way through the campaign, the Liberal Democrats dropped the policy of revoking Article 50 after the party realised it was not going to win a majority in the election.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-75)

The [Democratic Unionist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Unionist_Party "Democratic Unionist Party") was in favour of a withdrawal agreement in principle but opposed the deals negotiated by both May and Johnson, believing that they created too great a divide between Northern Ireland and the rest of the United Kingdom.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-76)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-77)[Sinn Féin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinn_F%C3%A9in "Sinn Féin"), the [Social Democratic and Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_and_Labour_Party "Social Democratic and Labour Party"), the [Ulster Unionist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_Unionist_Party "Ulster Unionist Party") (UUP),[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-cansteve-78) and the [Alliance Party of Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Party_of_Northern_Ireland "Alliance Party of Northern Ireland") all favoured remaining in the EU. The UUP did not see a second referendum as a necessary route to achieving this goal.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-cansteve-78)

#### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Environment")]

The Labour Party promised what they described as a green industrial revolution. This included support for renewable energies and a promise to plant 2 billion trees by 2040. The party also promised to transition to electrify the United Kingdom's bus fleet by 2030.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-79) The Liberal Democrats promised to put the environment at the heart of their agenda with a promise to plant 60 million trees a year. They promised to significantly reduce carbon emissions by 2030 and hit zero carbon emissions by 2045. By 2030, they planned to generate 80% of the country's energy needs from renewable energies such as solar power and wind and retrofit 26 million homes with insulation by 2030. They also promised to build more environmentally friendly homes and to establish a new Department for the Climate Crisis.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-80)

The Conservatives pledged net zero emissions by 2050 with investment in clean energy solutions and green infrastructure to reduce carbon emissions and pollution. They also pledged to plant 30 million trees and boost wind and solar energy.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-81)

#### Tax and spending commitments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Tax and spending commitments")]

In September 2019, the Conservative government performed a spending review, where they announced plans to increase public spending by £13.8 billion a year, and reaffirmed plans to spend another £33.9 billion a year on the [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_(England) "National Health Service (England)") (NHS) by 2023. Chancellor [Sajid Javid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajid_Javid "Sajid Javid") said the government had turned the page on 10 years of [austerity in the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austerity_in_the_United_Kingdom "Austerity in the United Kingdom").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-SpendGuard-82)

During the election, the parties produced manifestos that outlined spending in addition to that already planned. The [Conservative Party manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_manifesto "Conservative Party manifesto") was described as having "little in the way of changes to tax" by the [Institute for Fiscal Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Fiscal_Studies "Institute for Fiscal Studies") (IFS). The decision to keep the rate of corporation tax at 19%, and not reduce it to 17% as planned, was expected to raise £6 billion a year. The plan to increase the national insurance threshold for employees and self-employed to £9,500 would cost £2 billion a year.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS2-83) They committed to not raise rates of income tax, [National Insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Insurance "National Insurance"), or [VAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAT "VAT").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-ToryMan-84)

There were increased spending commitments of £3 billion current spending and £8 billion investment spending. Overall, this would have led to the country's debt as a percentage of GDP remaining stable. The IFS assessed that it would rise in the event of a no-deal Brexit.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS3-85) The [Labour Party manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_manifesto "Labour Party manifesto") planned to raise an extra £78 billion a year from taxes over the course of Parliament, with sources including:[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS2-83)

*   £24bn – raising the headline rate of corporation tax to 26%
*   £6.3bn – tax the global profits of multinationals according to the United Kingdom's share of global employment, assets, and sales, not British profits
*   £4.0bn – abolish patent box and R&D tax credit for large companies
*   £4.3bn – cutting unspecified corporation tax reliefs
*   £9bn – financial transactions tax
*   £14bn – dividends and capital gains
*   £6bn – anti-avoidance
*   £5bn – increases in income tax rates above £80,000 a year
*   £5bn – other

In addition, Labour was to obtain income from the Inclusive Ownership Fund, windfall tax on oil companies, and some smaller tax changes. There were increased spending commitments of £98 billion current spending and £55 billion investment spending. Overall, this would have led to the national debt as a percentage of GDP rising.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS3-85) Labour's [John McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McDonnell "John McDonnell") said borrowing would only be for investment and one-offs (e.g. compensating [WASPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WASPI "WASPI") women, not shown above), and not for day-to-day spending.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-DebtGuard-86)

The Liberal Democrats manifesto planned to raise an extra £36 billion per year from taxes over the course of Parliament, with sources including:[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS2-83)

*   £10bn – raising corporation tax to 20%
*   £7bn – 1% point rise in all rates of income tax
*   £5bn – abolish the capital gains tax allowance
*   £5bn – air passenger duty on frequent flyers
*   £6bn – anti-avoidance
*   £3bn – other

There were increased commitments of £37 billion current spending and £26 billion investment spending, which would overall lead to the debt as a percentage of GDP falling, partly due to improved economic conditions which would result from staying in the EU.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS3-85)

##### Institute for Fiscal Studies analysis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Institute for Fiscal Studies analysis")]

The [Institute of Fiscal Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Fiscal_Studies "Institute of Fiscal Studies") (IFS), an influential research body, released on 28 November its in-depth analysis of the [manifestos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifesto "Manifesto") of the three main national political parties.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSGuard-87)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSFinTimes-88) The analysis provided a summary of the financial promises made by each party and an inspection of the accuracy of claims around government income and expenditure.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS1-89)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSTimes-90)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFS2-83) The IFS reported that neither the Conservatives nor the Labour Party had published a "properly credible prospectus".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSGuard-87)

Its analysis of the Conservative manifesto concluded there was "essentially nothing new in the manifesto", that there was "little in the way of changes to tax, spending, welfare or anything else", and that they had already promised increased spending for health and education whilst in government. The Labour manifesto was described as introducing "enormous economic and social change", and increasing the role of the state to be bigger than anything in the last 40 years.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSTK-91)

The IFS highlighted a raft of changes in including free childcare, university, personal care, and prescriptions, as well as nationalisations, labour market regulations, increases in the minimum wage, and enforcing "effective ownership of 10% of large companies from current owners to a combination of employees and government". The IFS said that Labour's vision "is of a state not so dissimilar to those seen in many other successful Western European economies", and presumed that the manifesto should be seen as "a long-term prospectus for change rather than a realistic deliverable plan for a five-year parliament".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSTK-91) They said that the Liberal Democrats manifesto was not as radical as the Labour manifesto but was a "decisive move away from the policies of the past decade".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSGuard-87)

The Conservative manifesto was criticised for a commitment not to raise rates of income tax, National Insurance, or VAT, as this put a significant constraint on reactions to events that might affect government finances. One such event could be the "die in a ditch" promise to terminate the Brexit transition period by the end of 2020, which risked harming the economy.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSTK-91) The IFS also stated that it is "highly likely" spending under a Conservative government would be higher than in that party's manifesto, partly due to a number of uncosted commitments.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSGuard-87) Outside of commitments to the NHS, the proposals would leave public service spending 14% lower in 2023–2024 than it was in 2010–2011, which the IFS described as "no more austerity perhaps, but an awful lot of it baked in".[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#cite_note-IFSStand-92)

The IFS stated it had "serious doubt" that tax rises proposed would raise the amount Labour suggested, and said that they would need to introduce more broad based tax increases. They assessed that the public sector does not have the capacity to increase investment spending as Labour would want. The IFS further assessed the claim that tax rises would only hit the top 5% of earners as "certainly progressive" but "clearly not true", with those under that threshold impacted by changes to the marriage allowance, taxes on dividends, or capital gains, and lower wages or higher prices that might be passed on from corporation tax changes. On 12 December 2019,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-2) the [2019 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election") was held in Scotland, to elect all 650 members of the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom"), including the [59 Scottish seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Westminster_constituencies "Scottish Westminster constituencies").

It was held two and a half years after the previous [general election in June 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"). The Scottish National Party (SNP) received the most votes (45%, up 8.1% from the previous election) and won 48[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-hanvey-1) out of 59 seats—a gain of 13 over those won in 2017, and 81% of the Scottish seats in the House of Commons.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-3)

SNP gains came at the expense of both Labour and the Conservatives. The Tories remained the largest unionist party in Scotland even though they lost more than half of their Scottish seats, winning six compared to thirteen in 2017. Labour was reduced to only one seat, down from seven. The Liberal Democrats won four Scottish seats for no net change, although party leader [Jo Swinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Swinson "Jo Swinson") (herself the only major party leader to stand for election in Scotland) was unseated in her bid for re-election by her SNP challenger.

Labour's vote share was its lowest at a Westminster election in Scotland since December 1910.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-5)

## Political context

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Political context")]

The [June 2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election") in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") was fought in the aftermath of the [2016 Scottish Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Scottish_Parliament_election "2016 Scottish Parliament election"), in which the [SNP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party") won a third term in government but lost its overall majority in the Scottish Parliament (although the proportional electoral system at Holyrood was intentionally designed to make it very difficult for any one party to gain a majority). The [2016 EU referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_EU_referendum "2016 EU referendum") was held a month later on Thursday 23 June, and the final result was for the United Kingdom to leave the EU, although Scotland voted 62.0% Remain. Negotiations then began after the [invocation of Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_invocation_of_Article_50_of_the_Treaty_on_European_Union "United Kingdom invocation of Article 50 of the Treaty on European Union") in March 2017, which was expected to dominate the snap general election campaign.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-6)

In March First Minister Nicola Sturgeon called for a second independence referendum due to Scotland's vote to remain in the EU the previous year. The result was the issue dominated the 2017 general election and, although the SNP remained the largest party, their number of seats was much reduced, with the [Scottish Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Conservatives "Scottish Conservatives"), [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Labour "Scottish Labour") and the Liberal Democrats gaining a total of 21 seats.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-bbc.com-7) Former First Minister Alex Salmond and Westminster leader Angus Robertson were among those who lost their seats.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-bbc.com-7)

In the [2019 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom"), Scottish Labour lost its two MEPs, UKIP lost its seat, the SNP increased its number to three, the Scottish Conservatives held theirs and the [Brexit Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_Party "Brexit Party") and [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") gained one each.

### Television debates

Main article: [2019 United Kingdom general election §Television debates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election#Television_debates "2019 United Kingdom general election")

Like the rest of the United Kingdom, Scottish broadcasters hosted television debates. On 20 November, [BBC Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Scotland_(TV_channel) "BBC Scotland (TV channel)")'s flagship political programme, _[Debate Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debate\_Night "Debate Night")_, moderated by [Stephen Jardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Jardine "Stephen Jardine"), hosted a Young Voter's Special with representatives from the main parties where they debated in front of an audience of voters aged under 30. On 3 December, [STV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STV_(TV_channel) "STV (TV channel)") hosted a television debate moderated by [Colin Mackay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Mackay_(journalist) "Colin Mackay (journalist)")[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election_in_Scotland#cite_note-STV-11) and [BBC Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Scotland "BBC Scotland") announced that they would host a debate on 10 December, two days before the election, moderated by [Sarah Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Smith_(journalist) "Sarah Smith (journalist)").
